claims.canonicalWording: Generative AI is AI that produces content from a request and the material it is given—such as text, images, audio, video or code. It does that using patterns learned during training plus the context available for the current task.

teaching.mechanism: Patterns learned during training and current task context are used to produce content.
teaching.readerConsequence: Generation and verification are different jobs; generated content is not automatically evidence or a finished answer.
teaching.analogy: Carrie Bradshaw with a brief can write the column.
teaching.analogyLimit: The analogy describes generation, not truth, search, evidence or the whole AI product.
teaching.memoryLine: It can make the draft. It cannot make it true.

claims.evidenceSummary: NIST defines a class of AI models that generates derived synthetic content across several media.
limitations: Search and generation can be combined in one product.
The definition does not establish that output is accurate, sourced or fit for use.
recheckTriggers: A new LAiDIES episode proposes a competing definition.
AIDB or NewsStand surfaces a consequential primary-source change.

consumers.notes: New narration and released-audio integration remain required.
Local correction exists; Library admission hold remains.

correction.oldWording: Generative AI was defined through a permanent search-versus-writing split and 'first pass' shorthand.
correction.reason: The shorthand failed when products combine generation, retrieval and other tools.

claims.canonicalWording: A model is a trained component of an AI system that uses inputs to produce outputs. A model can be offered through an app, API or coding tool, while a larger product may combine it with instructions, memory, search, files, tools and other models.

teaching.mechanism: Training shapes the component; a larger system supplies inputs and may add other components and tools.
teaching.readerConsequence: Model capability, product features and account access are separate questions.
teaching.analogy: Episode 05 may use a fashion-house analogy only after the plain definition is ruled.
teaching.analogyLimit: A fashion analogy cannot imply that every product has one model or that a model exists only beneath a consumer app.
teaching.memoryLine: A model is part of the experience—not the whole thing.

claims.evidenceSummary: OECD describes models as core components of AI systems and notes that systems can combine one or more models.
limitations: Current provider examples and names require separate, dated provider evidence.
recheckTriggers: A standards body materially changes the model/system distinction.
Episode 05 or a class proposes a competing explanation.
A provider materially changes product/model naming or routing.

consumers.notes: Released narration still requires replacement and exact integration proof.

consumers.surface: Basics class: What these tools are

correction.oldWording: The model is the trained brain behind the app; products are magazines and models are editors-in-chief.
correction.reason: Models are not confined to apps, products may route among components, and the analogy conflicts with later curriculum.

claims.canonicalWording: A hallucination is false or unsupported content delivered as part of an AI-generated answer. It can be one invented citation, wrong date or made-up detail inside otherwise useful work—not only a completely fictional response.

teaching.mechanism: Generated content can diverge from evidence, input or earlier context while remaining fluent.
teaching.readerConsequence: A polished answer cannot be treated as evidence; consequential claims need source verification.
teaching.analogy: Every Burn Book entry in Episode 01 was invented and presented with total confidence.
teaching.analogyLimit: Requested fiction is not a hallucination, and the analogy must not suggest that some Episode 01 entries were true.
teaching.memoryLine: Polished is a style. Evidence is a standard.

products: All generative-AI learning and verification treatments

claims.evidenceSummary: NIST's confabulation risk includes false, erroneous, divergent or internally contradictory generated content; hallucination is retained as reader language.
limitations: No universal hallucination rate applies across tasks, models or evaluation methods.
The presence of retrieval or citations does not guarantee a grounded answer.
recheckTriggers: NIST revises the Generative AI Profile.
A surface uses a benchmark rate as a universal hallucination rate.
A derivative changes the Burn Book analogy.

consumers.notes: Competing wording remains and needs owner disposition.

correction.oldWording: The Burn Book was described as containing some true and some made-up entries; a benchmark range was presented as a universal hallucination rate.
correction.reason: The analogy contradicted episode canon and the benchmark measured a different failure mode.

claims.canonicalWording: The May 2026 version of HBS Working Paper 25-023 reports estimated generative-AI adoption of 47.8% for men and 39.3% for women among 318,924 respondents in sources reporting use by women and men—a 22% relative gap. The paper reports that the relative gap stabilized near 16% from early 2025.

teaching.mechanism: The working paper synthesizes 76 sources from more than 100 countries and compares reported use rates by gender where available.
teaching.readerConsequence: Participation helps shape which needs, defaults and uses receive attention; the statistic does not measure ability.
teaching.analogyLimit: Do not turn an average into a claim about every woman or man.
teaching.memoryLine: Women should not wait while AI is being shaped.

regions: More than 100 countries represented across synthesized sources

claims.evidenceSummary: The working paper reports the sample, estimated use rates, relative gap and time trend.
limitations: Working paper, not a final universal estimate.
Estimates vary by source, country, occupation and time.
The paper does not establish one universal cause.
recheckTriggers: HBS publishes a revised working-paper version or journal article.
New primary research materially changes the interpretation.
A derivative uses 25%, 78:100 or another superseded shorthand.
AIDB or NewsStand reports new gender-participation evidence.

consumers.notes: Cue source is corrected; exact released video requires rebuild/integration proof.

correction.oldWording: Women were described as using AI at 78% of men's rate or as having 25% lower adoption without the current paper version and scope.
correction.reason: The May 2026 working-paper version supplies the current sample, estimates and limits.

claims.canonicalWording: For common English text, one token is roughly 0.75 words, or about 1.3 tokens per word. This is a rule of thumb, not an exact conversion; counts vary by model, encoding and language.
claims.evidenceSummary: OpenAI states that one token is approximately four characters or three quarters of an English word and warns that tokenization varies.
limitations: The ratio is approximate and should not be used as an exact billing or context calculation.
Non-English text and different model encodings can produce different ratios.
recheckTriggers: OpenAI materially changes its token-counting guidance.
A LAiDIES consumer introduces a different numeric conversion.
A provider-specific lesson requires exact model tokenization.

consumers.notes: The rendered book intentionally keeps the safer non-numeric wording; it is consistent with this claim and does not restate the ratio.

correction.oldWording: The handbook reversed the relationship as 0.75 tokens per word.
correction.reason: OpenAI's rule of thumb is approximately 0.75 English words per token, equivalent to about 1.3 tokens per word.
